newsitem.title: USA: Dain Bosworth ups Smithfield on Taiwan pork news.
newsitem.headline: Dain Bosworth ups Smithfield on Taiwan pork news.

text.p: Key U.S. pork processor, Smithfield Foods will see rising pork exports due to a serious outbreak of hog disease in Taiwan that halted Taiwan's pork exports last month, broker Dain Bosworth said in a research alert on Thursday.
Dain Bosworth said it raised its rating on Smithfield to a buy from a hold and lifted its April 1997 Q4 earnings per share estimate to $0.70 from $0.35.
Dain also said it raised its EPS for full-year FY97 to $2.00 from $1.65 and for FY98 to $3.10 from $2.80.
"We view the hog disease problems in Taiwan, currently the largest exporter of pork to Japan, as a multi-year opportunity," Dain Bosworth analyst Bonnie Wittenburg said in the research update.

Taiwan on March 20 banned all exports of pork, saying an outbreak of foot and mouth disease in hogs had spread to epidemic proportions. On March 24 the government said it likely would take Taiwan five years to resume exports to Japan, where it had a 40-45 percent market share of pork imports.
Japan, South Korea and other Taiwan pork customers banned Taiwanese pork after the disease was announced.
Before the Taiwanese ban, only 22 percent of Japan's pork imports came from the United States, Wittenburg said.

"The disease outbreak, in our opinion, could forever change Taiwan's and America's market share in Japan. In the short run, perhaps two years, disease issues will keep Taiwan out of the Japanese market. In the long run, if the U.S. successfully seizes half to two-thirds of the Japanese market over the next couple of years, Taiwan may have great difficulty taking much of that back," Wittenburg said.
She also noted that South Korea may also look to the U.S. for pork.
Wittenburg said pork exports from Denmark, the world's largest pork exporter with an 18 percent market share as of 1995, present less of a challenge to the U.S. in East Asia.

"Countries in the Pacific Rim have steadily shown a preference for chilled, fresh pork, which works against Denmark and favors the United States because of better transportation logistics for the U.S. and because of U.S. technology for shipping chilled pork," Wittenburg said.
In 1995, Taiwan ranked second in world pork exports at 17 percent and the United States third at 16 percent.

Other supportive factors for pork producers in the U.S. include reports of scattered hog disease outbreaks in Europe, and the European Union/U.S. dispute over meat trade and meat inspection standards that faces an April 15 deadline.
The U.S. has threatened to ban European pork imports while European retaliation was expected to threaten shipments of U.S. eggs, dairy and poultry products, Wittenburg said.
The U.S. hog herd is likely to expand this year and in 1998 and added pork export demand will absorb some of the current excess slaughter capacity in the U.S., she said.
Smithfield's hot dog exports to Russia continue strong and strong pork demand through the Easter season also aided sales, the analyst added.
